name: GPGI, Inc.

profile.description: GPGI, Inc. (formerly CompoSecure, Inc.) is a multi-industry platform managed by Resolute Holdings Management under Executive Chairman David Cote (former Honeywell CEO), owning CompoSecure (premium metal payment cards for issuers such as American Express, U.S. Bank, Samsung and Klarna) and Husky Technologies (injection molding systems, aftermarket tooling and service for packaging and medical markets), combined in a $7.4B transaction completed in early 2026. Q2 2026 pro forma adjusted net sales were $473.2M (-4.1% YoY), with CompoSecure up 11.7% to $133.6M and Husky down 9.2% to $339.6M; pro forma adjusted EBITDA fell 12.5% to $113.9M. FY2026 guidance calls for $1.95-$2.1B of sales (flat organic) and $550-$610M of adjusted EBITDA, with net leverage of 3.9x targeted to fall to ~3.0x by year-end. The company is the subject of a securities class action and a derivative suit (Sullivan v. Cote) over the Husky deal and Resolute's fee of 10% of adjusted EBITDA.

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (2/3): The 2026 combination with Husky transformed CompoSecure from a single-product metal card maker into a multi-industry platform, and CompoSecure itself posted record Q2 2026 sales (+11.7%) with a 41.3% EBITDA margin on wins including Samsung, U.S. Bank's Amazon Business card and the Amex Delta SkyMiles Reserve relaunch [1]. AI Deployment (0/2): The Q2 2026 earnings presentation contains no references to AI, and no AI products or savings were found [1]. Market Share (1/2): CompoSecure is a meaningful premium metal card supplier with five ICMA Élan awards in 2026, but no share data was disclosed, and Husky's sales fell 9.2% on customer delays [1]. Product Pipeline (1/2): Management cites a 'robust and growing pipeline' at Husky and a new London Design Center for international card expansion, without quantified launch timelines [1]. R&D Intensity (0/1): R&D spending is not disclosed at the GPGI level.

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (1/4): GPGI's stated identity centers on applying the Resolute Operating System as a 'proven playbook across platforms' to acquired businesses — an operating formula rather than a purpose [1]. Community Impact (0/2): No distinctive community or charitable programs were found. Employee Retention (0/2): Husky's CEO and CFO departed around the January 2026 close, and management describes an 'aggressive' cultural change underway at Husky [1][4]. Insider Buying (2/2): Form 4s show meaningful open-market buying in 2026 — officer/director Thomas Knott bought 44,000 shares at $17.08 in March and 85,250 shares at $11.67 in June (~$1.75M combined), with additional purchases by officer Kurt Schoen and directors John Cote, Kevin Moriarty, Krishna Mikkilineni and Rebecca Loree, versus one director sale of 13,667 shares [5].

infrastructure.label: DEVELOPING
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored for the Growth sleeve on available metrics. Forward P/E of 8.9x meets the target and FMP's forward PEG of 1.84 (2x weight) earns partial credit, but ROE of -20.6% (2x weight) and a negative profit margin score zero — the margin of about -20.7% is derived from the H1 2026 GAAP net loss of $184.7M against ~$894M of H1 pro forma sales [1][3][6]. Q2 pro forma sales declined 4.1% YoY. Debt-to-equity is excluded as not meaningful: the listed parent accounts for Husky/GPGI Holdings under the equity method and shows no debt, while the operating entity carries $2.115B of debt (3.9x net debt/EBITDA); the 5-year revenue CAGR is excluded because the merger makes history non-comparable [1][3]. Liquidity floor cleared: ~1.58M shares x $11.18 = ~$17.7M daily.

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (7/9): Both businesses make physical products — precision metal payment cards and injection molding systems, tooling and service for packaging and medical manufacturers — that AI cannot substitute, and no analyst commentary found flags AI as a risk [1]. Husky's ~40% aftermarket tooling and 25-30% service mix ties revenue to installed equipment, though card demand faces longer-term pressure from digital wallets (a non-AI substitution risk), keeping the score in the PROTECTED band. AI Opportunity (0/1): No AI-related revenue or AI initiatives are disclosed [1].

infinite_game.summary: Through Sinek's lens, GPGI is a textbook finite construct: an acquisition vehicle whose external manager is paid 10% of adjusted EBITDA, built to compound EBITDA through deals and an operating playbook rather than to pursue a cause. Insider buying shows conviction in the financial plan, but the governance structure, leadership turnover at Husky and pending fraud litigation point to a company playing to win the next deal, not to keep playing.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (0/3): GPGI articulates no vision of a better future; its identity is the Resolute Operating System applied to acquired platforms, and the Resolute management fee equal to 10% of annual adjusted EBITDA aligns the manager with EBITDA growth rather than any cause [1][2].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): Husky's CEO and CFO departed at the deal close and management describes an 'aggressive' cultural change at Husky, suggesting a top-down transformation rather than a circle of safety [1][4].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): No management commentary was found framing competitors as benchmarks for self-improvement; communications focus on program wins, margins and leverage targets [1].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): CompoSecure reinvented itself from a single-product card maker into a diversified platform by combining with Husky [2]. Sinek would note the change was driven by deal-making and fee economics rather than a Just Cause, and it added $2.1B of debt and a business now declining 9%.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (0/2): Recent decisions — a debt-funded $7.4B acquisition and a fee structure tied to EBITDA — prioritize financial engineering over long-term capability, and the short seller's allegations that Husky's value was inflated to win shareholder approval are now the subject of litigation [2][4].

investment_thesis: CompoSecure is a high-quality franchise: Q2 2026 adjusted net sales hit a record $133.6M (+11.7%) at a 41.3% EBITDA margin, with new programs for Samsung, U.S. Bank, Amex Delta SkyMiles Reserve and Klarna and a London Design Center supporting international growth [1]. Management reiterated FY2026 guidance of $550-$610M adjusted EBITDA (+7% at the midpoint, margin up 120bps) and $275-$325M of free cash flow, targets deleveraging from 3.9x to ~3.0x by year-end, and insiders bought roughly $1.75M of stock in 2026 [1][5]. At ~8.9x forward earnings, the stock prices in significant skepticism about Husky.
thesis_continued: Husky drives the risk: Q2 sales fell 9.2% and EBITDA 22.6% on customer delays, tariffs and resin volatility, pulling consolidated pro forma EBITDA down 12.5% [1]. The balance sheet carries $2.1B of debt, the six-month GAAP net loss was $184.7M, and governance is contentious — Resolute (controlled by the Cote family) earns 10% of adjusted EBITDA, and both a securities class action (class period November 3, 2025 to May 6, 2026) and the Sullivan v. Cote derivative suit allege the Husky deal was overvalued [1][2][4]. The stock has fallen from $19.74 before the Jehoshaphat report to ~$11 [4].
key_catalysts: Husky second-half recovery: management cites order growth and a 'robust and growing pipeline' to support 2H 2026 margin expansion via ROS fixed-cost leverage [1]
Deleveraging from 3.9x to ~3.0x net debt/EBITDA by year-end 2026, supported by $275-$325M of guided free cash flow [1]
CompoSecure international expansion through the London Design Center and new issuer programs (Samsung, Klarna, Kast, DolarApp) [1]
key_risks: Husky cyclicality: Q2 2026 sales -9.2% and EBITDA -22.6% on customer delays, tariffs and oil/resin volatility; guided to decline low-to-mid single digits in FY2026 [1]
Governance and litigation: securities fraud class action and Sullivan v. Cote derivative suit over the Husky valuation and Resolute's 10%-of-EBITDA management fee [2][4]
Leverage of $2.115B of debt (3.9x net debt/EBITDA) at the operating entity limits flexibility if Husky's recovery stalls [1]
